component_findings.dependency_declaration: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Direct dependencies can be declared explicitly at an appropriate project/module boundary rather than inferred from ambient state. Evidence basis: Assessment of language-level dependency semantics for Rust, independent of Cargo ecosystem maturity (which belongs to Ecosystem evaluation). | Rust programs reviewed under /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/rust/micro (mb00.rs through mb11.rs) are self-contained, relying only on the Rust standard library (std::collections, std::io, std::fmt, etc.) with no external crate dependencies required for core micro-benchmark logic. | Rust's module system (mod, use, pub) provides explicit, unambiguous dependency declaration at the language level: every external symbol used must be explicitly brought into scope via use, and crate dependencies are declared once in Cargo.toml with semantic versioning enforced by Cargo.lock rather than manual header/linker bookkeeping. | No global mutable namespace pollution: Rust has no implicit global includes or preprocessor-based conditional dependency inclusion (unlike C/C++ #include and #ifdef chains), reducing accidental coupling. | Cargo's dependency resolution is deterministic and reproducible via Cargo.lock; Rust has no stable ABI to break, each crate is recompiled from source with monomorphization, and binaries are statically linked by default, so what you use is what you link. | Feature flags (Cargo features) allow fine-grained optional dependency inclusion via Cargo.toml + #[cfg(feature = ...)] keeping unused dependency code out of the final bi…

component_findings.artifact_source_separation: Recertified level 4 under the current criterion: Source-level program meaning is not unnecessarily tied to a single compiler ABI, filesystem convention or host-specific build assumption. Evidence basis: Assessment of Rust's language/compiler design for platform neutrality, independent of the breadth of currently realized supported platforms (an Ecosystem concern). | Rust's std library is explicitly layered (core/alloc/std) allowing targeting freestanding, no_std, and embedded environments without any language changes -- a first-class, deliberate portability design feature. | The micro-benchmark programs reviewed (mb00.rs-mb11.rs) use only std::collections, std::time, std::fmt and similar platform-neutral APIs with no OS-specific syscalls or inline asm, demonstrating that idiomatic Rust code naturally stays portable. | Cross-compilation is a designed-in compiler feature (rustc --target, cargo build --target) backed by LLVM, letting a single toolchain target many architectures/OSes from one host. | Conditional compilation via #[cfg(target_os = ...)], #[cfg(target_arch = ...)] is a structured, compiler-checked mechanism for platform-specific code paths, rather than textual preprocessor hacks. | Rust has no undefined/implementation-defined ABI reliance for typical safe code; memory layout guarantees (repr(C) opt-in) make FFI/portability explicit and opt-in rather than accidental. | Rust does not mandate a garbage collector or heavyweight managed runtime, so it can target bare-metal and WASM equally well; realized platform breadth itself is scored separately under Ecosystem.
